title:
The State of Quantum Computing:​
Applications, Initiatives, Challenges and Ethical Concerns 
up to 2025
abstract_summary: This systematic review surveys experimental and commercial quantum computing work from 2016–2025, documenting applications across sectors (agriculture, defense, energy, finance, healthcare, infrastructure, manufacturing, and technology), representative demonstrations and tools, and government and multilateral initiatives. It synthesizes reported outcomes and benchmarks, and discusses major technical challenges (cost, scalability, limited problem applicability, workforce shortages, and accessibility) as well as ethical concerns including cryptographic risks, access disparities, military uses, socioeconomic impacts, and environmental sustainability.
methodology_description: The paper reports a systematic literature review (SLR) methodology to synthesize existing knowledge on quantum computing use cases across industries (2016–2025). The authors queried multiple sources, including peer-reviewed journals (Springer, Frontiers, Nature), open-access repositories (arXiv), company blogs/case studies/white papers from major quantum vendors, and government publications. Search queries combined keywords such as "quantum computing applications," "quantum computing use case," "quantum technology cooperation," "quantum computing limitations," and "quantum computing initiatives." Inclusion criteria restricted sources to publications from 2016–2025 that focus on experimental and commercial use cases of quantum computing; exclusion criteria removed non-English items and articles lacking official sources or peer review. The SLR aimed to map domains of usage, methods, tools, initiatives, inter-governmental cooperation, quantified results, and limitations.

key_findings: [supported] Quantinuum and Mitsui conducted a trial transmitting 'quantum tokens' over a 10 km fibre network in Tokyo demonstrating unforgeable transaction tokens based on quantum physical principles.

[supported] HSBC and IBM demonstrated a quantum-enabled algorithmic bond trading proof-of-concept (RFQ optimization) using IBM's Heron processor, reporting up to a 34% improvement in prediction accuracy on production-scale trading data.

[supported] D-Wave's Advantage2 hybrid solver is reported (vendor datasheet/press) to handle optimization problems with up to approximately 2 million variable constraints and is commercially available via cloud.

[supported] Quantum-safe communication and QKD deployments are operational in some real-world networks (e.g., Toshiba's Quantum Secure Metro Network in London), indicating active deployment of quantum cryptography technologies.

[speculative] Quantum computing is framed as a near-term frontier for unlocking new algorithms in dynamic financial challenges (e.g., trading and routing) rather than a far-off future technology; hybrid quantum-classical approaches are emphasized as the current practical path.

[supported] Quantum-enhanced random number generation (Quantinuum 'Quantum Origin') claims specific high-entropy and reuse properties, and is presented as a deployable service to strengthen cryptographic entropy sources.

[speculative] Theoretical quantum primitives (e.g., no-cloning theorem) underpin claims that quantum tokens can prevent double-spending and forgery; trials show feasibility of transmission but system-level economic/operational security claims remain theoretical until broader deployments and audits.

[supported] The review documents multiple government- level investments and strategies in quantum technologies (aggregate figures cited: global investment > $55.7 billion as of 2025) implying strong public-sector support that will influence industry capabilities, including finance.

[supported] There are documented, narrow empirical demonstrations of quantum/hybrid methods improving particular operational problems (e.g., logistics, routing, bidding/quote optimization) relevant to financial services workflows.

[speculative] While Shor's algorithm theoretically threatens current public-key cryptography, large-scale practical breaking of widely deployed crypto remains contingent on fault-tolerant, large-qubit machines and thus is a credible future risk rather than an immediate empirically realized threat.

[supported] Many reported finance and fintech experiments employ hybrid quantum-classical pipelines (e.g., QAOA/VQE combined with classical optimizers) rather than standalone large-scale quantum algorithms, reflecting the NISQ-era practical pattern.

[supported] The review lists concrete operational limitations and challenges relevant to finance adoption: high development/operational cost, limited problem applicability, restricted geographic/access availability, and shortage of specialized workforce.

[speculative] Ethical and socioeconomic concerns are highlighted (cryptography/privacy risks, access disparities, military applications, job displacement, environmental sustainability); these are plausible policy/ethical risks but not empirical outcomes demonstrated within the cited finance experiments.

[supported] Vendor and laboratory benchmark/demonstration claims (e.g., Google Sycamore / Willow supremacy-type results; D-Wave commercial solver capabilities) are reported and used by industry actors to motivate finance experiments, though their direct translation to broad financial advantage is case-dependent.
results_summary: The review reports several concrete, small-to-medium scale empirical demonstrations of quantum or hybrid quantum-classical methods applied to finance-relevant problems: a Quantinuum-Mitsui trial of quantum tokens over 10 km of fibre, and an HSBC–IBM proof-of-concept showing up to 34% improved prediction accuracy in an RFQ bond-trading optimization using IBM's Heron processor. Vendors (D-Wave, Quantinuum, IBM) and governments have invested heavily and are providing cloud-accessible services and hybrid solvers (D-Wave Advantage2, Quantinuum's services, IBM's stack) that enable experimentation. However, most finance use-cases remain narrow, hybrid, and demonstrative rather than broadly transformative; real, general-purpose quantum advantage across financial services is not yet established. The review also emphasizes cryptographic risks (future threat from Shor-type algorithms), advances in quantum-safe tools (QKD, QRNG), and practical barriers—cost, workforce, limited applicability, and ethical/legal concerns—that constrain adoption.
performance_claims: Quantinuum and Mitsui transmitted quantum tokens across a 10 km fibre network (trial).
HSBC–IBM quantum-enabled RFQ optimization reported up to 34% improvement in prediction accuracy on production-scale trading data.
D-Wave's Advantage2 hybrid solver reported capability to tackle up to ~2,000,000 (2 million) variable constraints (vendor claim).

Quantinuum's Quantum Origin QRNG: reported min-entropy ~0.85 from three-qubit entangled circuits, distilled to near-ideal randomness with error probability as low as 2^-128, and a reusable Quantum Seed that can be shared/reused up to 2,300 times (vendor claims).
Global public and private investment in quantum technologies cited as > $55.7 billion as of 2025 (aggregate figure cited in review).

Google's Willow chip (vendor claim) with 105 qubits completed a random-circuit benchmark in under five minutes versus an estimated 10^25 years on the world's fastest classical supercomputer (vendor extrapolation reported in the review).
quantum_advantage_detail: The review documents narrow empirical demonstrations where hybrid quantum-classical approaches yielded measurable improvements for specific finance tasks (e.g., HSBC–IBM RFQ optimization), but these are case-by-case, vendor/experiment-specific, and do not establish a broad, general-purpose quantum advantage across financial services. Most real-world deployments are hybrid, limited in scope, and dependent on vendor benchmarks and proprietary tooling; thus, broader claims of general quantum advantage in finance remain speculative pending reproducible, industry-wide demonstrations on economically material problems.

contradictions: contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The review collects strong vendor/industry claims of advantage (e.g., D-Wave Advantage2 scalability, HSBC–IBM 34% RFQ improvement) alongside cautions and caveats that these are narrow, vendor-supplied, or case-dependent results rather than general superiority over classical methods.

contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — Theoretical threats (Shor) are presented as imminent risks by some actors but the review emphasises current infeasibility without fault-tolerant, large-qubit machines, creating tension between policy/cryptography urgency and technical reality.
